name: TCS NQT (Ninja, Digital, Prime)
tagline: One national test that routes you to TCS Ninja, Digital or Prime offers

overview.about: TCS hires most freshers through the TCS National Qualifier Test (NQT), delivered on TCS iON. A single test with a Foundation and an Advanced section decides which track you are considered for: Ninja (Foundation scores), or Digital and Prime (Advanced section, higher packages). Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.
eligibility: B.E./B.Tech/M.E./M.Tech/MCA/M.Sc from the batches named in the notification
Typically 60% or more in 10th, 12th/diploma and graduation (as reported; check current notice)
Active backlogs must be cleared before joining; education-gap limits apply as per notice
Register on TCS NextStep and apply for the NQT drive before the deadline

pattern.paper: Part A — Foundation: Numerical, Verbal, Reasoning
pattern.note: Clears you for Ninja; sections are individually timed
Hidden test cases; choose C/C++/Java/Python etc.
Technical + Managerial + HR, often one panel

overview.frequency: NQT cycles run several times a year; dates are announced on TCS NextStep

cards.title: One test, three outcomes
cards.body: You don't apply separately for Ninja and Digital any more. Everyone takes the NQT; your section scores decide whether you are interviewed for Ninja, Digital or Prime. Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Foundation section
cards.body: Numerical ability, verbal ability and reasoning ability, each with its own timer. Easy-to-moderate questions from the aptitude syllabus. Strong Foundation scores alone can get a Ninja interview.

cards.title: Advanced section
cards.body: Advanced quantitative and reasoning MCQs plus an advanced coding section (2–3 problems, about 90 minutes). This is what makes you eligible for Digital and Prime.

cards.title: The three tracks
points: Ninja: entry-level developer role, Foundation-based
Digital: higher package, needs good Advanced + coding scores
Prime: highest fresher package, for top NQT performers
Packages change every year — read the offer details on the official page

cards.title: Timed sections
cards.body: Once a section's timer ends (or you submit it), you usually cannot return to it. Budget time per question and don't leave easy marks on the table.

cards.title: Strategy
cards.body: Aim to clear Foundation comfortably first, then push in the Advanced section. Solve at least one coding problem fully (all test cases) rather than two problems partially.

cards.q: Which part of the NQT makes you eligible for TCS Digital or Prime?
cards.explain: Digital and Prime are decided by Advanced-section performance, followed by interviews.

cards.q: Where do candidates register for the TCS NQT hiring process?
cards.explain: Use the official TCS NextStep portal; TCS never charges recruitment fees.

notes.p:
The **TCS National Qualifier Test (NQT)** is one test that decides which hiring track you are considered for. You register on **TCS NextStep**, apply for the drive, and take the test on **TCS iON** (at a centre or remotely, depending on the drive). Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

The paper has two parts. **Part A — Foundation** (≈ 65 questions, ≈ 75 minutes) covers **Numerical Ability**, **Verbal Ability** and **Reasoning Ability**, each in its own timed section. **Part B — Advanced** has **Advanced Quantitative & Reasoning** (≈ 15 questions, ≈ 25 minutes) and **Advanced Coding** (2–3 problems, ≈ 90 minutes).

Your **Foundation** score makes you eligible for **Ninja** interviews. Strong **Advanced** section scores (especially coding) make you eligible for **Digital** or **Prime** interviews, which carry higher packages and more demanding technical interviews. You do not choose the track yourself — the scores do — so attempt the Advanced section seriously even if you are aiming for Ninja.
points: Ninja: Foundation-based shortlisting; interview covers basics, project and HR.
Digital: good Advanced scores; deeper coding, DSA and CS fundamentals.
Prime: top Advanced scores (usually solving coding problems fully); toughest interview.
Exact cut-offs are not published and vary by drive.

notes.p: Because each section is **individually timed** and you usually cannot return to a finished section, plan time per question and move on when stuck. No negative marking has been reported in recent NQT drives, so never leave a question blank — but confirm in your drive's instructions.
points: **Numerical:** percentages, ratio, time-work, TSD, number system, mensuration, probability; use the on-screen calculator only for heavy arithmetic.
**Verbal:** sentence completion, error spotting, para-jumbles, reading comprehension; read questions before the passage.
**Reasoning:** series, coding-decoding, seating, blood relations, data sufficiency, statement–conclusion.
**Advanced Q&R:** fewer but harder questions; skip anything taking over 2 minutes and return if time remains.
**Coding:** read input from STDIN exactly as described; print only the required output.

notes.p:
**Numerical.** A shopkeeper marks a phone 25% above cost and gives a 12% discount. Profit%? 1.25 × 0.88 = 1.10 → **10% profit**.

**Reasoning.** Series: 4, 9, 19, 39, 79, ? Each term = previous × 2 + 1 → **159**.

**Verbal.** 'Each of the students ____ submitted the assignment.' Answer: **has** ('each' is singular).

**Advanced quant.** How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by 3 or 5 but not by 15? By 3: 333, by 5: 200, by 15: 66. By 3 or 5 = 333 + 200 − 66 = 467; remove multiples of 15 → **401**.
Use this if you are starting late:
points: Week 1: core aptitude formulas and 30 timed questions a day.
Week 2: verbal and reasoning practice; one sectional mock every two days.
Week 3: coding — arrays, strings, math problems, reading input correctly; 2 problems a day.
Week 4: full mocks under NQT timing; review every wrong answer.
Throughout: keep a mistake notebook and revise it before the test.
One test decides Ninja, Digital or Prime eligibility.
Foundation: numerical, verbal, reasoning — separately timed.
Advanced: harder Q&R plus coding; it decides Digital/Prime.
Attempt everything if no negative marking is announced.
Practise on a similar test interface and with STDIN input.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Numerical style
cards.body: Short calculation questions: percentages, ratios, time-work, speed, P&C, probability, data interpretation tables. Expect 1–2 minutes each.

cards.title: Sample numerical
cards.body:
Q: A sum doubles in 5 years at simple interest. In how many years does it become 4 times?
SI for 5 years = P → rate 20%. To gain 3P you need 15 years.

cards.title: Verbal style
cards.body: Sentence completion, error spotting, reading comprehension, para-jumbles and word usage. Read each RC question before the passage.

cards.title: Reasoning style
cards.body: Number/letter series, coding-decoding, blood relations, seating arrangement, statement–assumption, data sufficiency and visual reasoning.

cards.title: Sample data sufficiency
cards.body:
Q: Is x even? (1) x² is even. (2) x is a multiple of 3.
(1) alone: x² even ⇒ x even (for integers) → sufficient. (2) alone: 3 or 6 → not sufficient. Answer: statement 1 alone.

cards.title: Sample advanced quant
cards.body:
Q: How many 3-digit numbers are divisible by 7?
First 105, last 994 → (994 − 105)/7 + 1 = 128.

cards.title: Practise on the real interface
cards.body: TCS iON tests use an on-screen interface with a timer per section. Take at least two full-length timed mocks before the test day.

cards.q: A sum doubles in 4 years at simple interest. The rate is:
How many 2-digit numbers are divisible by 6?
Is integer n odd? (1) n + 1 is even. (2) n² is odd. Which is sufficient?
cards.explain: Both (1) and (2) independently force n to be odd.

notes.p: TCS questions are mostly **moderate difficulty but time-bound**: the challenge is speed and accuracy, not tricks. Questions are often wordy; underline the numbers and what is asked. Many numerical questions are **fill-in-the-blank** (type the answer) rather than multiple choice in some drives, so you cannot guess from options. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

**Q1 (ages).** The ratio of ages of A and B is 4 : 5. After 5 years it will be 5 : 6. Find A's age. (4x + 5)/(5x + 5) = 5/6 → 24x + 30 = 25x + 25 → x = 5 → **A = 20 years**.

**Q2 (clocks).** Angle between the hands at 3:40? Angle = |30H − 5.5M| = |90 − 220| = **130°**.

**Q3 (counting).** How many 3-digit numbers are divisible by 7? ⌊999/7⌋ − ⌊99/7⌋ = 142 − 14 = **128**.

**Q4 (work).** A does a job in 12 days and B in 18. They work together for 4 days, then A leaves. Total = 36 units, A = 3/day, B = 2/day. In 4 days: 20 units; remaining 16 units by B: 8 days. **Total 12 days.**

**Q5 (statement–conclusion).** Statement: 'All trains to Delhi are cancelled today because of dense fog.' Conclusion I: Dense fog can disrupt train services. Conclusion II: No train to Delhi will run tomorrow. I is directly supported by the reason given; II talks about tomorrow, which the statement does not cover. **Only I follows.**

**Q6 (data sufficiency).** Is x even? (1) 3x is even. (2) x + 1 is odd. Statement 1 alone: 3x even ⇒ x even (for integers). Statement 2 alone: x + 1 odd ⇒ x even. **Each alone is sufficient.**

**Q7 (para-jumble).** Find the opening sentence (introduces a topic, no unexplained pronoun), then link by pronouns and connectors such as 'however' and 'as a result'.

**Q8 (sentence completion).** 'The manager was ____ about the deadline; she would not allow any extension.' Options: lenient / adamant / casual. Answer **adamant** — the second clause explains the blank.

When practising, verify your answers with tiny programs — it also builds coding speed for the Advanced section:

`x = next(x for x in range(1, 50) if 6 * (4 * x + 5) == 5 * (5 * x + 5))
print("A =", 4 * x)
print(abs(30 * 3 - 5.5 * 40))
print(999 // 7 - 99 // 7)
print(sum(1 for n in range(1, 1001) if (n % 3 == 0 or n % 5 == 0) and n % 15 != 0))`

Output:
`A = 20
130.0
128
401`

points: Typing units or extra spaces in fill-in-the-blank answers when only a number is expected.
Spending too long on one question in a timed section.
Data sufficiency: solving fully instead of only checking sufficiency.
Statement–conclusion: using outside knowledge instead of the statement.
Not rounding as instructed (e.g. 'correct to two decimal places').
Speed + accuracy beats difficult tricks.
Expect typed-answer numerical questions in some drives.
Clock angle = |30H − 5.5M|.
Count multiples with floor division.
Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together.
Practise with a timer every day.

cards.title: Coding environment
cards.body: You read input from standard input and print to standard output. Hidden test cases check edge cases; output format must match exactly — no extra prompts like 'Enter n'.

cards.title: Typical easy problem
cards.body:
Print the sum of digits of each number in a list.
n = int(input())
for _ in range(n):
    x = input().strip().lstrip('-')
    print(sum(int(d) for d in x))

cards.title: Typical topics
points: Arrays & strings: rotations, frequency, palindromes
Math: primes, GCD, digit manipulation
Greedy and simple DP for Advanced coding
Sorting with custom rules

cards.title: Technical interview
cards.body: Expect: your final-year project in depth, one language (OOP), DBMS/SQL queries, OS basics, a small code on paper, and why you chose your stream.

cards.title: Managerial & HR
cards.body: Managerial checks situational judgement and attitude ('your teammate misses deadlines…'). HR covers relocation, shifts, documents and your interest in TCS.

cards.title: Read the problem twice
cards.body: Most failed test cases come from ignoring constraints (n up to 10⁵, negative numbers, empty input). Test with the sample and one edge case before submitting.

cards.q: In the TCS coding round, your program should:
options: Read from standard input and print only the required output
Read from a file named input.txt
cards.explain: Extra text breaks automated output matching.

cards.q: Which is most likely in a TCS technical interview for freshers?
options: Designing a distributed database from scratch
Only puzzles with no technical questions
Explaining your project and writing a small program
cards.explain: Fresher technical rounds focus on fundamentals and your own work.

notes.p:
The Advanced Coding section gives **2–3 problems in ≈ 90 minutes** on the TCS iON compiler with languages such as C, C++, Java and Python. Your code is judged on **hidden test cases**, so it must handle edge cases and read input **exactly** in the stated format from STDIN. Do not print prompts like 'Enter a number'. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

Typical difficulty: the first problem is easy-to-medium (arrays, strings, math), the second medium-to-hard (greedy, sorting, DP, simulation). Solving the first fully and the second partially can still help; solving both is usually needed for Prime.

**Problem.** Given a lowercase string, print each distinct character followed by its count, in order of first appearance.

`from collections import Counter

s = input().strip()
freq = Counter(s)
print("".join(ch + str(freq[ch]) for ch in dict.fromkeys(s)))`

Sample input:
`aabccca`

Output:
`a3b1c3`

`dict.fromkeys(s)` keeps distinct characters in first-seen order. Time **O(n)**, space O(k) for k distinct characters.

notes.h: Sample problem 2: sum of primes up to N
notes.p:
**Problem.** Read N (up to 10⁶) and print the sum of all primes ≤ N. Checking each number by trial division is too slow for large N; use the **Sieve of Eratosthenes**.

`n = int(input())
is_prime = [True] * (n + 1)
is_prime[0] = is_prime[1] = False      # assumes n >= 2
i = 2
while i * i <= n:
    if is_prime[i]:
        for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):
            is_prime[j] = False
    i += 1
print(sum(i for i in range(n + 1) if is_prime[i]))`

Sample input:
`20`

Output:
`77`

Primes up to 20 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, which sum to 77. The sieve runs in **O(N log log N)** time and O(N) space.

The interview is often one panel with **Technical (TR)**, **Managerial (MR)** and **HR** parts, lasting 30–60 minutes. Digital/Prime interviews go deeper into DSA, OOP, DBMS and your projects.

**TR: 'Explain your final-year project.'** A: Problem, your role, tech stack, one challenge and how you solved it, result — in two minutes.

**TR: 'Difference between C and Java?'** A: C is procedural, compiled to machine code, manual memory; Java is object-oriented, compiled to bytecode for the JVM, garbage-collected.

**MR: 'The client changes requirements a day before delivery. What do you do?'** A: Understand the change, estimate impact, inform the lead, agree on priority and a revised timeline in writing.

**HR: 'Are you comfortable with relocation and shifts?'** A: Answer honestly; TCS posts freshers across India.

points: Read STDIN exactly; print only the answer.
Test edge cases: empty input, N = 1, large N.
Use efficient methods (sieve, hashing, sorting).
Interview: TR + MR + HR, often in one panel.
Know your project and resume line by line.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.
